source.title_on_document: Neural Mechanisms of Collaborative Creative Thinking in Engineering Design: Human-Human Versus Human-AI Interaction

supplement.where: No supplementary material or online appendix is referred to in the chapter, and none is included in the PDF (PDF pp. 1-9, including back matter and references on pp. 8-9). The word 'Supplement' on PDF p. 9 is part of reference [13].
supplement.holds: No supplementary-only statistics are identified. For the idea ratings, the text reports two Wilcoxon p-values (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3), and Fig. 2 shows condition means as bars without numeric arm means (PDF p. 6). Numeric arm means, SDs, and Wilcoxon test statistics are not printed.

paper_design_summary: The study analyzed ideas from 14 male engineering students who each completed an open-ended engineering design task alone, with another participant, and with GPT-4 (PDF pp. 3-5, Sects. 2.1, 2.3, and 3). Condition order was counterbalanced between subjects, with randomization not stated, and EEG was recorded during the task. Two creativity researchers rated the ideas for originality and usefulness on five-point scales, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests compared conditions (PDF pp. 4-5, Sects. 2.4 and 3).

studies.label: Within-subject EEG experiment: engineering design ideation alone, with a human partner, and with GPT-4

assignment.what_was_assigned: The order of the three conditions (Individual, Human-Human, Human-AI). Every participant did all three conditions. The paper says the order was counterbalanced between subjects and never says it was randomized.
assignment.quote: All experimental participants performed the following three conditions. The order of implementation of the conditions was counterbalanced between subjects.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 330), Sect. 2.3 Conditions; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 2.4 ('within-subject design')

arms.name: Individual
arms.description: An engineering design task requiring divergent thinking, performed by a single individual on their own. In the idea recognition phase the participant read their own idea.

arms.name: Human-Human
arms.description: Two persons performed the engineering task (two participants took part in each session). Each participant typed an idea in the idea output phase and read the partner's idea in the idea recognition phase.

arms.name: Human-AI
arms.description: An individual performed the engineering task with the help of AI (GPT-4). In the idea recognition phase the participant read the AI's idea.

participants.exclusions: None reported. Sect. 2.1 describes fourteen participants, and Sect. 3 reports scores for 'the 14 participants'. Every participant did all three conditions, so the same 14 people contribute to every arm.
participants.who: Male engineering students, healthy with no brain-related diseases or disabilities, all right-handed (Japanese version of the Flanders Handedness Test). Two participants took part in each session. The number of sessions is not stated.
participants.country: not_stated (the evidence points to Japan: approval by the Research Ethics Review Committee of the University of Tokyo, handedness measured with the Japanese version of the Flanders Handedness Test, and authors at the University of Tokyo and Ricoh, Tokyo)
participants.quote: Fourteen male students of engineering participated in this study. All students were healthy with no brain-related diseases or disabilities; two participants participated in each experiment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 330), Sect. 2.1 Participants; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3

ai_tool.how_used: In the Human-AI condition an individual performed the task 'with the help of AI (GPT-4)'. Each idea cycle had a 30 s thinking phase, a 30 s typing phase, and a 10 s idea recognition phase in which the participant read the AI's idea. The paper does not say how the AI's ideas were produced, what prompt was used, or whether participants could query GPT-4 freely. The role code is the best fit to this description. Source: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 331), Sect. 2.3, Conditions and Task.

task.description: Open-ended engineering design task requiring divergent thinking, taken from Hay et al. (2019): original product solutions to societal problems, for example a product that reduces the space needed to store glass products at home before recycling. Flow per problem: (1) problem recognition (reading the problem, no duration given), (2) divergent thinking (30 s), (3) idea output (typing the idea, 30 s), (4) idea recognition (reading one's own, the partner's, or the AI's idea, 10 s). Phases (2) to (4) were repeated 10 times for each problem. Source: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 331), Sect. 2.3, Task; reference [14] on PDF p. 9 (printed p. 336).
task.duration: Each cycle includes 30 s of divergent thinking, 30 s of idea output, and 10 s of idea recognition; these phases were repeated 10 times per problem. No duration is given for problem recognition, and the number of problems per condition is not stated. All procedures, including electrode attachment and removal, were designed to finish within two hours (PDF p. 4, printed p. 331, Sect. 2.3, Task).

outcomes.name: Usefulness of ideas (5-point expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two creativity researchers rated the ideas on a five-point scale for usefulness to society as a whole, based on whether they thought the idea reasonable and useful. The printed scale labels contain an apparent typo ('5. very much so,' '4. very much so,' '3. very much so,' '2. slightly so,' '1. not at all') (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 331-332, Sect. 2.4). Fig. 2 shows mean scores by condition for ideas from the 14 analyzed participants; conditions were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3; PDF p. 6, Fig. 2). The observation unit entered into the tests is not stated, so unit is null. The paper also does not state how the two raters' scores were combined, inter-rater agreement, the number of ideas, or what the error bars show.

contrasts.reported: Wilcoxon signed-rank test: 'the usefulness score was higher in the Human-AI condition than in the individual condition (p = 0.023)'. Fig. 2 (bottom panel) marks this pair with * (p < 0.05). Fig. 2 prints no numeric arm means, and the paper prints no means, SDs, or test statistics. Error bars are of unstated type. n = 14 analyzed participants in each condition (within-subject).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2 bottom panel

contrasts.reported: No result is printed for this pair. Fig. 2 (bottom panel) shows the two bars at similar heights with no significance marker. Text: 'the usefulness scores were higher in the human-human and human-AI conditions compared to the individual condition.' For reference, Human-Human vs Individual: 'the usefulness score tended to be higher than in the individual condition (p = 0.084)', marked † (p < 0.1) in Fig. 2. n = 14 analyzed participants.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2 bottom panel

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas (5-point expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two creativity researchers rated the ideas on a 5-point scale from '1. not original at all' to '5. very original', judging whether an idea was an intelligent response others could not come up with and could not be imagined from the usual way of using things (PDF p. 4, printed p. 331, Sect. 2.4). The paper reports using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for originality and usefulness, but gives no originality p-value (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3). Fig. 2 shows mean scores by condition (PDF p. 6). The observation unit entered into the tests is not stated, so unit is null. The paper also does not state how the two raters' scores were combined, inter-rater agreement, the number of ideas, or what the error bars show.

contrasts.reported: Text: 'The originality scores did not differ between conditions.' No p-value, means, or SDs are printed. Fig. 2 (top panel) shows the three bars at similar heights with no significance marker. Error bars are of unstated type. n = 14 analyzed participants.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2 top panel

contrasts.reported: Text: 'The originality scores did not differ between conditions.' No p-value, means, or SDs are printed. Fig. 2 (top panel) shows no significance marker for this pair. n = 14 analyzed participants.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2 top panel

eligibility.reason: Only 14 people were analyzed, with the same people completing all three conditions; this is below the 50-person threshold (PDF p. 3, printed p. 330, Sects. 2.1 and 2.3; PDF p. 5, printed p. 332, Sect. 3; PDF p. 6, printed p. 333, limitations). Criterion 1 is unclear: 'The order of implementation of the conditions was counterbalanced between subjects.' The paper does not state that this order was allocated randomly (PDF p. 3, Sect. 2.3). Criterion 3 is met because two creativity researchers rated the originality and usefulness of participants' generated ideas (PDF p. 4, printed p. 331, Sect. 2.4). The study belongs in the screening report as an experiment below the sample-size threshold. Clarifying randomization would not change its core exclusion.

one_line_finding: Among 14 engineering students analyzed in a within-subject EEG study, ideas produced with GPT-4 were rated more useful than ideas produced alone (Wilcoxon p = 0.023), while originality did not differ across conditions (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3; PDF p. 6, Fig. 2).
open_questions: Whether the counterbalanced condition order was allocated randomly (PDF p. 3, Sect. 2.3). This affects criterion 1, although the 14-person analyzed sample already rules out core eligibility.

Who prompted GPT-4, what prompts were used, and whether participants could query it freely beyond reading its idea during idea recognition (PDF p. 4, Sect. 2.3). These details would refine the ideas_supplied role code; generative-AI assistance itself is explicit.

The observation unit of the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, how the two raters' scores were combined, and what the Fig. 2 error bars show (PDF pp. 4-6, Sects. 2.4 and 3, Fig. 2). The test name and participant count do not establish the analysis unit.
notes: PDF pages 1-9 are printed pages 328-336. The paper's main outcomes are EEG source-localization (eLORETA) contrasts during the idea-thinking phase (Fig. 3, PDF p. 7). They are not scored on the output and are not listed. The paper has no diversity outcome and no outcome after AI removal. Fig. 2 prints no numeric arm means; no values were estimated from its bars. Screener A's eye-read bar heights are left out under form rules 1 and 8. Neither outcome is named primary. Under codebook rule 8.2, originality (novelty rated by people) would come before usefulness. The abstract says collaboration, 'regardless of the partner type, significantly enhanced the usefulness of generated ideas', but Sect. 3 gives p = 0.084 for Human-Human vs Individual ('tended to be higher'). The paper cites Liu et al. (2024, 'When ChatGPT is gone') as reference [11] but analyzes only its own 14 participants. Finalizer audit: the complete nine-page markdown, including the references, was read; there are no appendices in this PDF. No c122 challenge files were present, so challenge_resolution is empty and its action counts are zero. The seven reconciliation differences are all marked resolved; that object is preserved unchanged. Final coding supersedes its unsupported lab_rct and participant-unit assumptions: design_class is other because randomization is not established (PDF p. 3, Sect. 2.3), and both outcome units are null because the Wilcoxon observation unit is not reported (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3). Task duration records only the printed phase durations and repetition count, replacing the unprinted total per cycle (PDF p. 4, Sect. 2.3).

open_items.item: Random allocation of the counterbalanced condition order is not stated (PDF p. 3, Sect. 2.3). The authors' allocation procedure would settle criterion 1; the 14-person analyzed sample still excludes this study from the core.

Who prompted GPT-4, the prompts used, and whether participants could query it freely are not reported (PDF p. 4, Sect. 2.3). The authors' protocol would settle the AI-role details. These do not affect an eligibility criterion because assistance from GPT-4 is explicitly stated.

The Wilcoxon observation unit, aggregation of the two researchers' ratings, and meaning of the Fig. 2 error bars are not stated (PDF pp. 4-6, Sects. 2.4 and 3, Fig. 2). The authors' analysis description would settle these details; the creativity outcomes are explicitly scored on participants' ideas, so criterion 3 is already met.
